data.overview: Adidas AG, the German sportswear giant (revenue €23.683 billion in 2024, HQ Herzogenaurach), publishes extensive company sustainability disclosures including CSRD/ESRS-aligned annual reports, a Restricted Substances Policy, animal-derived materials standards, and binding supplier Workplace Standards. Independent assessments are mixed: Good On You rated Adidas "Not Good Enough," citing a 2021 French greenwashing ruling and labour concerns, and Ethical Consumer flags workers'-rights and animal-welfare issues, while BrandScore gives it a "B+ Good" overall score.

claims.claim: Adidas maintains a Restricted Substances Policy prohibiting chemicals considered harmful or toxic and reviews it annually.
claims.quote: we adopted a comprehensive and detailed Restricted Substances Policy ("A-01 Requirements") for product materials, prohibiting the use of chemicals considered as harmful or toxic

claims.claim: Adidas aims to source animal-derived materials humanely and ethically, considering animal welfare and species conservation.
claims.quote: adidas aims to source materials of animal origin in a humane, ethical, and sustainable manner concerning animal welfare and species conservation

claims.claim: Adidas commits to no deforestation, conversion or degradation in the supply chains it sources from.
claims.quote: adidas is committed to no deforestation, conversion and degradation in the supply chains which we source from, and to the protection and restoration of biodiversity and ecosystems

claims.claim: Adidas imposes contractually binding Workplace Standards on suppliers covering health, safety, and labour rights, and has a zero-tolerance stance on forced labour.
claims.quote: The Workplace Standards are contractually binding requirements applicable for our suppliers’ factories, covering health and safety, labor rights and environmental protection.

papers.title: How Ethical Is Adidas?
papers.summary: Good On You's April 2024 rating (based on a November 2023 'Not Good Enough' assessment) found Adidas set a science-based emissions target but is not on track to meet it, lacks published biodiversity and deforestation policies, and was penalised for a 2021 French advertising ruling that its '50% recycled' Stan Smith campaign misled consumers. Its labour rating dropped to 'Not Good Enough'.

findings.text: Adidas has set a science-based emissions target but is not on track to meet it.
findings.quote: while Adidas has set a target to reduce greenhouse gas emissions generated from its own operations and supply chain, it’s not on track to meet this target

findings.text: A French advertising jury ruled Adidas's '50% recycled' Stan Smith campaign misled consumers, a case Good On You calls greenwashing.
findings.quote: Adidas’ “Stan Smith Forever. 100% iconic, 50% recycled” campaign broke advertising rules and misled consumers

findings.text: Good On You found no evidence Adidas has policies to protect biodiversity in its supply chain.
findings.quote: We also found no evidence Adidas has policies to protect biodiversity in its supply chain—another key issue in our methodology.

findings.text: Adidas's labour rating dropped from 'It's a Start' to 'Not Good Enough' in its most recent rerate.
findings.quote: Adidas’s labour rating has unfortunately dropped from “It’s a Start” to “Not Good Enough” in its most recent rerate, indicating it’s falling behind on critical industry issues.

papers.title: How ethical is Adidas AG?
papers.summary: Ethical Consumer's profile (last updated November 2025) flags several ethical issues with Adidas, including paying high executive wages while garment workers earn below basic needs, likely tax-avoidance strategies, greenwashing accusations, and animal-welfare concerns. It cites Covid-era factory non-payment and a 2021 Public Eye report on Cambodian garment workers.

findings.text: Adidas is criticised for high executive pay while supply-chain garment workers are not paid enough for basic needs.
findings.quote: paying excessively high wages to executives, while failing to pay garment workers in the supply chain enough to cover even basic needs

findings.text: Adidas was linked to factories refusing to pay workers when they shut during the Covid-19 pandemic.
findings.quote: The company was linked to major violations during the Covid-19 pandemic, after factories refused to pay workers when they shut down due to the pandemic.

findings.text: Ethical Consumer notes likely tax-avoidance strategies and animal-welfare concerns.
findings.quote: Other issues include likely use of tax avoidance strategies, accusations of greenwashing and concerns over animal welfare.

papers.title: Is Adidas a Good Company? Ethics, Sustainability & Ratings (2026)
papers.summary: BrandScore gives Adidas an overall 'B+ Good' score, praising ISO 14001 certification since 2010, UN Global Compact participation, and product certifications (FSC, RDS, RWS). It flags at least three environmental violations related to greenwashing claims and a Trustpilot rating of 1.5/5 indicating poor customer satisfaction.

findings.text: Adidas holds ISO 14001 certification since 2010 and participates in the UN Global Compact.
findings.quote: ISO 14001 certified since 2010, indicating strong environmental management. ✓ Active participant in the UN Global Compact, showing commitment to sustainability.

findings.text: BrandScore found at least three environmental violations related to greenwashing claims.
findings.quote: At least 3 environmental violations found related to greenwashing claims. ! Trustpilot rating of 1.5/5 indicates poor customer satisfaction.

findings.text: Adidas holds product certifications including FSC, RDS and RWS for responsible sourcing.
findings.quote: Holds multiple product certifications like FSC, RDS, and RWS, ensuring responsible sourcing.

papers.title: adidas Sustainability Report 2025 breakdown
papers.summary: This plain-English review concludes Adidas is one of the more auditable large-scale sportswear companies in 2025, publishing a downloadable, report-grade Sustainability Statement that makes claims easier to trace. However, it stresses Adidas remains a high-volume, high-footprint business, so 'credible disclosure' is not the same as 'low impact,' and decoupling volume from footprint is not yet proven.

findings.text: Adidas is described as more auditable than many footwear peers due to its structured, downloadable disclosure package.
findings.quote: adidas is one of the more auditable large-scale sportswear companies in 2025 reporting, but it still operates a high-volume, high-footprint model

findings.text: The review notes strong disclosure does not offset the large absolute footprint of high-volume footwear.
findings.quote: even strong climate disclosure cannot hide the fact that high-volume footwear has a large absolute footprint

findings.text: It flags that Adidas has not yet proven product volume and absolute footprint are decoupling.
findings.quote: clearer proof that product volume and absolute footprint are decoupling stronger, more legible circularity systems beyond limited programs

legalMatters.title: French JDP ruling on 'Stan Smith Forever' recycled claim
legalMatters.summary: France's advertising jury (JDP) ruled that Adidas's '50% recycled' Stan Smith campaign broke advertising rules and misled consumers over recycled content.
legalMatters.quote: According to the French Jury de Déontologie Publicitaire (JDP), Adidas’ “Stan Smith Forever. 100% iconic, 50% recycled” campaign broke advertising rules and misled consumers.
